# IB EconLens — full text of the free guides

> IB EconLens turns weekly global current affairs into IB Diploma Economics revision guides. Each guide gives background, argument breakdown, vocabulary, chart reading, three exam-labelled tasks and model answers with marks notes, with the IB syllabus unit labelled. This file contains the full text of the free guides only. Subscriber guides are not included. Site: https://ibeconlens.geledtech.com/ — see llms.txt for the site map.

## A shortage of sulphur could hurt mines and farms everywhere (Sample Volume 01)

# IB EconLens: Single 1 of 5

**Paper 1 (a) · 10 marks** · **Paper 2** · **IA · 14 marks**

# A shortage of sulphur could hurt mines and farms everywhere

Finance and economics, 17 October 2026 issue.

IB unit: Microeconomics: 2.2 Supply, 2.3 Competitive market equilibrium. *Also useful:* Macroeconomics: 3.3 Cost-push inflation.
Exam link: trains Paper 1 (a) (10 marks) + Paper 2 data response + IA (micro commentary, 14 marks). Paper 3 not covered by this guide.
What it argues. A war-driven squeeze on refining has produced a quieter second shock: sulphur, a by-product input for fertiliser, mining and chipmaking, is scarce, and the damage is only beginning to show.

Before you read. Sulphur is a by-product of refining, so a refining squeeze is automatically a sulphur squeeze. Russia had already banned sulphur exports, cutting shipments from 4.8 million tonnes in 2025 to 1.8 million tonnes in 2026 so far. In February, Middle Eastern sulphur fetched USD 500 a tonne, up from USD 340 a year earlier. The Strait of Hormuz closure trapped nearly a quarter of global production and half of seaborne exports; shipments remain two-thirds below pre-war levels.

Key vocabulary.
- by-product: something produced in the course of making something else.
- fertiliser: a substance added to soil to help crops grow.

How to read it.
- Reading note. The author opens with diesel, the shock readers already understand, then pivots to sulphur, its quieter side-effect. The pivot builds a causal chain — war, refineries cut off, fuel squeeze, then sulphur starved — and reframes the crisis as an input story, wider than the price at the pump.

A war-driven squeeze on refining has produced a quieter second shock: sulphur, a by-product input for fertiliser, mining and chipmaking, is scarce, and the damage is only beginning to show.
Tasks.
- A. Paper 1 (a) · 10 marks. Use a supply-and-demand diagram to explain how the sulphur shortage pushes up the price of fertiliser.
- B. Paper 2 data response. The article states that sulphur markets were already tight before the war. What does that do to a simple "the war caused it" reading? Name the two causes a good commentary must keep separate.
- C. IA commentary (800 words) — IA · 14 marks. Using this article as your extract, analyse the effect of the sulphur shortage on the market for fertiliser, with a supply-and-demand diagram. Evaluate one possible response, such as a subsidy to fertiliser producers or a strategic stockpile.

## Model answers (read after attempting the tasks)

Task A model. Sulphur is an input in fertiliser production, so a shortage raises producers' costs of production. On a supply-and-demand diagram for fertiliser, the supply curve shifts left, from S1 to S2. The equilibrium price rises from P1 to P2 and the equilibrium quantity falls from Q1 to Q2. The size of the price rise depends on the elasticity of demand: fertiliser has few short-term substitutes and is essential for crop yields, so demand is price-inelastic. The price therefore rises proportionately more than quantity falls, and farmers' total spending on fertiliser increases even though they buy less. The article's figures show the mechanism at work: Middle Eastern sulphur reached USD 500 a tonne, up from USD 340 a year earlier, while the Strait of Hormuz closure trapped nearly a quarter of global production. A leftward supply shift caused by higher input costs is exactly what the diagram shows.

Marks: 9–10 band — the diagram is fully explained, the shift is correctly linked to higher input costs, terminology is accurate throughout, and the article's figures are used as evidence. It would fall to the 7–8 band if the diagram were drawn but not explained, or if the elasticity reasoning were left out.

Task B model. Two causes must be kept separate. First, pre-war tightness: Russia had already banned sulphur exports, cutting shipments from 4.8 million tonnes in 2025 to 1.8 million tonnes in 2026 so far, Prices had already risen from USD 340 to USD 500 a tonne before the Hormuz closure. Second, the war shock itself: the Strait's closure trapped nearly a quarter of global production and half of seaborne exports, leaving shipments two-thirds below pre-war levels. The distinction matters because the two causes imply different durations and remedies: a war shock may reverse with a ceasefire, but structural tightness will not.

Marks: 5/5 (Paper 2 short answer) — the two causes are separated with precise figures and the distinction is tied to duration and remedy. It would lose a mark if it only listed the causes without explaining why keeping them apart matters.

Task C model: IA commentary. *Key concept: scarcity.* Sulphur is scarce in the strict sense: a by-product of refining, its supply cannot be raised just because fertiliser makers want more of it. When refining is squeezed, the scarce input must be rationed, and in a market the price does the rationing. Sulphur is an input in fertiliser production, so the shortage raises producers' costs. On a supply-and-demand diagram for fertiliser (Figure 1), the supply curve shifts left, from S1 to S2. The equilibrium price rises from P1 to P2 and the equilibrium quantity falls from Q1 to Q2. Because fertiliser is an essential input with few short-term substitutes, demand for it is relatively price-inelastic: the price rise is proportionately large while the quantity fall is small, so farmers' total spending on fertiliser rises even as they use less of it — the higher price decides who still gets fertiliser and who goes without.

Figure 1 — The market for fertiliser. Price (P) vertical, quantity (Q) horizontal. D1 slopes down, S1 slopes up, meeting at E1 (P1, Q1). Higher costs shift supply left to S2; new equilibrium E2 (P2, Q2).

The effects spread beyond the diagram, and scarcity decides who bears them. Farmers face higher costs and thinner margins; some cut fertiliser use, which lowers crop yields and tightens food supply further. Consumers then face higher food prices. The burden is uneven: low-income households spend a larger share of income on food, so a fertiliser-driven food price rise hits them hardest — the rationing falls on those least able to pay.

Can policy fix this? A subsidy to fertiliser producers would cushion farmers, but it burdens the government budget and does not increase the supply of sulphur itself: it hides the price signal that rations a scarce input rather than easing the scarcity. Strategic stockpiles would address scarcity directly, but they are slow and costly to assemble, and cannot be created after the shortage has arrived.

The evaluation, then, is mixed. Government action can cushion the blow, especially for the poorest consumers, but it cannot cure a physical shortage: protect vulnerable households while supply adjusts, rather than pretending the price signal can be wished away.

Marks: 13/14 — A 3/3 (Figure 1 drawn, fully labelled, explained in the text), B 2/2, C 3/3, D 3/3 (scarcity named and carried through), E 2/3 (the case for intervention is thinner than the case against — the lost mark). Strength: inelastic demand tied to who the rationing falls on.

## Another warning sign for China's economy: falling consumer credit (Sample Volume 01)

# IB EconLens: Single 2 of 5

**Paper 1 (a) · 10 marks** · **Paper 2** · **IA · 14 marks**

# Another warning sign for China's economy: falling consumer credit

Finance and economics, 17 October 2026 issue.

IB unit: Macroeconomics: 3.2 AD/AS, 3.3 Macroeconomic objectives.
Exam link: trains Paper 1 (a) (10 marks) + Paper 2 data response + IA (macro commentary, 14 marks). Paper 3 not covered by this guide.
What it argues. Chinese households are borrowing less and spending less, despite government efforts to loosen their purse-strings — a warning sign for domestic demand.

Before you read. Short-term loans to consumers fell by 8.3% in September, the steepest drop on record. In August the stock of consumer loans was the lowest since the harsh zero-covid lockdowns. During a public holiday at the start of October, the typical holidaymaker spent 2% less than a year earlier. Household debt stood at 60% of GDP in 2020 and has since declined slightly (rich countries as a whole are just below 70%). The property crash means fewer mortgages and early repayments. The finance ministry has been subsidising banks so they can charge lower interest on consumer loans for big-ticket items.

Key vocabulary.
- frugal: careful with money, reluctant to spend.
- purse-strings: control over spending (to loosen them is to encourage spending).
- mortgage: a loan used to buy a home.
- subsidy: a payment by government that lowers a cost or price.

How to read it.
- The article sets a policy (subsidised loan rates) against an outcome (falling credit). What would you need to know before judging whether the policy failed?
- Reading note. The author builds the 'warning sign' from data, not mood: the 8.3% fall in short-term consumer loans is the steepest on record, the August loan stock is the lowest since the zero-covid lockdowns, and holiday spending fell 2%. A record break turns a vague impression of frugality into a measurable break with the past, and the spending figure confirms the borrowing data reflect real spending.

Chinese households are borrowing less and spending less, despite government efforts to loosen their purse-strings.
Tasks.
- A. Paper 1 (a) · 10 marks. Use an AD/AS diagram to explain how falling consumption affects real output and the price level in China.
- B. Paper 2 data response. "Households are borrowing less because they are frugal." The article offers this explanation and then qualifies it. State the qualified version in your own words, without letting "frugal" carry the whole explanation.
- C. IA commentary (800 words) — IA · 14 marks. Using this article as your extract, analyse the effect of falling consumption on aggregate demand, with an AD/AS diagram. Evaluate the interest-rate subsidy policy: why might cheaper loans fail to raise borrowing?

## Model answers (read after attempting the tasks)

Task A model. Consumption is the largest component of aggregate demand, so falling consumption shifts aggregate demand left, from AD1 to AD2, on an AD/AS diagram. Real output falls from Y1 to Y2 and the price level comes under downward pressure, from P1 to P2. Unemployment is likely to rise as firms cut production in response to weaker demand. The fall is amplified by the multiplier: lower spending means lower incomes for others, who then spend less in turn, so the final fall in output is larger than the initial fall in consumption. The article's evidence fits the diagram: short-term consumer loans fell 8.3% in September, the steepest drop on record, and holiday spending fell 2%. The mechanism is a demand-side contraction, not a supply shock: the economy moves down along the aggregate supply curve as demand falls.

Marks: 9–10 band — the AD shift is correctly linked to consumption, the output, price-level and unemployment effects are all stated, the multiplier is explained, and article data are used. It would fall to the 7–8 band if only the shift were stated without its consequences, or if the diagram were left unexplained.

Task B model. Households are borrowing less, but frugality is only part of the story. The property crash has cut mortgage demand and encouraged early repayment, and a mortgage is the largest loan most households take on, so that alone would shrink total borrowing. Consumer credit, however, has fallen even though the finance ministry subsidises banks to charge lower interest on loans for big-ticket items such as cars and renovations. If cheaper loans cannot lift borrowing, the cause is more likely weak confidence about incomes and house prices, or banks reluctant to lend, than a simple change in household character. The article's qualified version is therefore: borrowing is falling because demand is weak and credit conditions are tight, not merely because households have become careful.

Marks: 5/5 (Paper 2 short answer) — mortgage and consumer credit are separated, the subsidy evidence is used, and a qualified version is stated. It would lose a mark if it accepted "frugal" uncritically.

Task C model: IA commentary. *Key concept: interdependence.* Consumption is the largest component of aggregate demand, so falling consumption shifts aggregate demand left, from AD1 to AD2, on an AD/AS diagram (Figure 1). Real output falls from Y1 to Y2, the price level comes under downward pressure, from P1 to P2, and unemployment is likely to rise as firms cut production. The multiplier is interdependence in action: one household's spending is another's income, so lower spending means lower incomes for others, and the final fall in output is larger than the initial fall in consumption. The article's evidence fits the diagram: short-term consumer loans fell 8.3% in September, the steepest drop on record, and holiday spending fell 2%.

Figure 1 — Aggregate demand and aggregate supply in China. Price level (P) vertical, real output (Y) horizontal. AD1 slopes down, SRAS slopes up, meeting at E1 (P1, Y1). Falling consumption shifts aggregate demand left to AD2; new equilibrium E2 (P2, Y2).

The policy response struggles because it works only through a chain of linked decisions, and any weak link breaks it. First, cheaper loans help only if households want to borrow, and with house prices falling and incomes uncertain, confidence, not the interest rate, is the binding constraint. Second, banks may pocket the subsidy or lend only to the safest borrowers, so transmission is weak. Third, the subsidy targets big-ticket items while the weakness is broad-based. The property market is linked too: the crash cuts mortgage demand and encourages early repayment, shrinking borrowing before confidence is even counted. Direct transfers would likely do more, since lower-income households spend a higher share of extra income, but they cost the budget and add to government debt. The policy treats a demand problem as a price problem: it may help at the margin, but it cannot by itself reverse a confidence-driven contraction, because the contraction runs through the links between households, banks and firms.

Marks: 14/14 — A 3/3 (Figure 1 drawn, fully labelled, explained in the text), B 2/2, C 3/3, D 3/3 (interdependence named and carried through — multiplier, policy transmission, property-credit link), E 3/3 (three limits plus the transfers alternative, with its cost noted). Strength: the evaluation tests the policy against the real constraint, confidence. Watch-point: the transfers alternative is sketched, not costed — the closest thing to a lost mark.

## Lessons from Britain's humiliating IMF bail-out (Sample Volume 01)

# IB EconLens: Single 3 of 5

**Paper 1 (a) · 10 marks** · **Paper 2** · **Paper 1 (b) · 15 marks**

# Lessons from Britain's humiliating IMF bail-out

Britain, 17 October 2026 issue.

IB unit: The global economy: 4.5 Exchange rates, 4.6 Balance of payments.
Exam link: trains Paper 1 (a) (10 marks) + Paper 2 data response + Paper 1 (b) essay (15 marks). Paper 3 not covered by this guide.
What it argues. The year 2026 echoes 1976, but the parallels are superficial: another trip to the IMF is unlikely, because the fundamentals are very different.

Before you read. In 1976, sterling's freefall forced Chancellor Denis Healey to turn back from a plane on 28 September and apply for an emergency IMF loan. A USD 3.9 billion bail-out, agreed in December, imposed conditions normally reserved for the world's weakest economies. Then: inflation 13.7%, ten-year gilt yields 15.7%, marginal tax rates as high as 98%. Now: inflation 3.8% (IMF estimate), ten-year gilt yields 5.4%, though Britain pays more to borrow than any other G7 country.

Key vocabulary.
- bail-out: an emergency loan or rescue for a government, bank or firm in trouble.
- gilt: a British government bond.
- yield: the return a bond pays its holder, as a percentage of its price.
- sterling: the British pound.
- fiscal: relating to government revenue and spending.

How to read it.
- The 1976-versus-2026 comparison does the persuading. Pick two pairs of numbers and state, in one sentence each, what each pair proves.
- Reading note. The 1976 parallel works emotionally before it works logically: a Chancellor turning back from a plane primes the reader to fear repetition. The article then tests the parallel against fundamentals — inflation 13.7% then against 3.8% now, gilt yields 15.7% against 5.4% — so the reader arrives worried and leaves reassured. A reader who stops at the parallel carries away a fear the evidence does not support.

The year 2026 echoes 1976, but the parallels are superficial.
Tasks.
- A. Paper 1 (a) · 10 marks. Use a foreign-exchange market diagram to explain how a loss of confidence in sterling can cause the pound to depreciate.
- B. Paper 2 data response. "In both years the embattled Labour Party appointed a new prime minister." Is this evidence of an economic parallel, or a coincidence? How do you tell the difference?
- C. Essay — Paper 1 (b) · 15 marks. "A country that issues its own currency cannot face a 1976-style crisis." Evaluate this claim, using the article's evidence. TOK extension: is historical analogy a valid form of economic evidence, and what are its limits?

## Model answers (read after attempting the tasks)

Task A model. On a foreign-exchange market diagram for sterling, the price of the pound is set by demand for and supply of sterling. A loss of confidence makes investors sell sterling-denominated assets, increasing the supply of sterling on the market and reducing demand for it. The supply curve shifts right and the demand curve shifts left, so the exchange rate falls from E1 to E2: sterling depreciates. Depreciation raises the price of imports, which pushes up inflation, and it raises the cost of servicing foreign-currency debt. The article shows why confidence matters: in 1976 sterling's freefall forced Britain to seek a USD 3.9 billion IMF loan, while in 2026 inflation of 3.8% and gilt yields of 5.4% are far below 1976 levels, so the same mechanism has produced a much smaller fall. The diagram explains the direction of the effect; the scale depends on the fundamentals.

Marks: 9–10 band — both curves are shifted in the right directions, depreciation and its consequences (import prices, inflation) are stated, and article evidence is used to show the scale. It would fall to the 7–8 band if only one curve were shifted, or if depreciation were asserted without its consequences.

Task B model. It is a coincidence, not economic evidence. The test is mechanism: does the fact transmit economic pressure? A shared party, a new prime minister two years into office, even a shared surname (Healey) describe political timing; they do not move bond yields, the exchange rate or inflation. The economic parallels, bond yields, inflation, competitiveness, energy shocks, do carry causal weight, because each one affects borrowing costs, purchasing power or trade. Confusing the two is the classic correlation trap: narrative resemblance is not an economic mechanism, and an argument built on it will collapse as soon as the mechanisms are examined.

Marks: 5/5 (Paper 2 short answer) — the mechanism test is applied cleanly: political timing is separated from what moves yields, the exchange rate or inflation. It would lose a mark if it treated narrative resemblance as evidence.

Task C model: essay. A government that issues its own currency borrows in that currency, so it cannot be forced to default in the way a foreign-currency borrower can. The central bank can always buy government bonds, as it did in 2008 and during the pandemic. On this view, a 1976-style crisis, understood as running out of money, is close to impossible.

The case against is strong, however. A currency can still fall sharply, raising import prices and inflation. Bond markets can demand much higher yields, raising debt-service costs: Britain already pays more to borrow than any other G7 country. Markets judge credibility, and an IMF programme is often about credibility rather than cash: a government may not need the money but may need the market to believe it will act. Figure 1 shows the mechanism: a loss of confidence shifts demand for sterling left and supply right, so the exchange rate falls from E1 to E2 even though the government issues the currency. The two shifts reinforce the fall in the rate and roughly offset each other on quantity.

Figure 1 — The foreign-exchange market for sterling. Exchange rate vertical, quantity (Q) horizontal. D1 slopes down, S1 slopes up, meeting at E1. A loss of confidence shifts demand left to D2 and supply right to S2; new equilibrium E2, a lower exchange rate.

Britain has lived this: in September 2022 the mini-budget destroyed market confidence, gilt yields spiked, sterling fell to a record low against the dollar, and the Bank of England had to intervene to buy gilts. No default was threatened, yet the government still had to reverse its budget within weeks. That is a 1976-style crisis in modern form — not running out of money, but running out of credibility. The article's own evidence points this way. Inflation and yields are far below 1976 levels, yet borrowing costs are still the highest in the G7, which suggests markets are pricing risk, not just fundamentals.

The defensible conclusion is therefore weaker than the claim. "Cannot" is too strong; "less likely, and different in form" is the version the evidence supports. As a TOK extension: historical analogy is useful for generating hypotheses, watch bond yields, watch sterling, but weak as proof, because it selects similarities and hides differences. It is valid only when the underlying mechanisms match, not merely the surface features.

Marks: 13–15 band (Paper 1 (b)) — theory is complete on both sides, real examples are effective (2008, the pandemic, the September 2022 mini-budget, G7 borrowing costs), evaluation is balanced with a judgement, structure is clear, and Figure 1 is used effectively to show the depreciation mechanism. Closest gap: the 1976 comparison is not re-tested against the 2022 case, whose cause was fiscal credibility rather than an external deficit. The TOK extension carries no Paper 1 marks. Strength: the "cannot" versus "less likely" distinction.

## China is channelling much more money to poor countries (Sample Volume 01)

# IB EconLens: Single 4 of 5

**Paper 1 (a) · 10 marks** · **Paper 2** · **Paper 1 (b) · 15 marks**

# China is channelling much more money to poor countries

China, 17 October 2026 issue.

IB unit: The global economy: 4.7 Sustainable development, 4.10 Development strategies.
Exam link: trains Paper 1 (a) (10 marks) + Paper 2 data response (alternative prompt) + Paper 1 (b) essay (15 marks). Paper 3 not covered by this guide.
What it argues. As America steps back from multilateral giving, a gap opens; China, though giving more, is neither willing nor able to fill it, while seeking a greater say in the institutions that hand aid out.

Before you read. America has tired of the institutions it helped create: last year the aid it channelled through multilateral organisations such as the World Bank and the UN fell by half, it has withdrawn from the World Health Organisation, and it still owes the WHO money. China has put up more cash, but cautiously. The article frames it with the historian Charles Kindleberger's idea: danger arises when a stabilising power gives up its global role before an emerging power is ready or willing to take it on.

Key vocabulary.
- multilateral: involving several countries or international organisations together.
- assertiveness: confident, forceful behaviour.
- arrears: money owed and overdue.
- think-tank: an institute that researches policy questions.
- channel: to direct money or resources through a particular route.

How to read it.
- The argument rests on who gives what, through which institutions. Before judging the conclusion, map the actors: the US, China, the World Bank, the UN, the WHO.
- Reading note. The opening names two traps, then sets one aside: the Thucydides trap (rivalry) is discarded so the Kindleberger trap (a stabiliser stepping back before a successor is ready) lands harder. The discarded frame reframes the story from competition to gap, and signals the author's stance — rivalry would at least be energetic, while the actual danger is a vacuum.

As America steps back from multilateral giving, a gap opens.
Tasks.
- A. Paper 1 (a) · 10 marks. Use a diagram to explain why global public goods, such as disease control, are under-provided when multilateral funding falls.
- B. Paper 2 data response. "China is giving more" and "China cannot fill the gap" sound contradictory. Reconcile them in two sentences, using the article's focus on multilateral channels.
- C. Essay — Paper 1 (b) · 15 marks. Using this article as your extract, evaluate whether multilateral aid is more effective than bilateral aid for development. Or, as a Paper 2 question: discuss the view that aid is driven by donor interests rather than recipient needs.

## Model answers (read after attempting the tasks)

Task A model. Disease control is a global public good: it is non-rival and non-excludable, so the market provides too little of it. On a diagram, the marginal social benefit (MSB) of disease control lies above the marginal private benefit (MPB), because countries other than the one paying also gain. The market provides quantity Qm, where MPB equals marginal cost, but the socially optimal quantity is Qs, where MSB equals marginal cost, so Qs is greater than Qm: the good is under-provided. When multilateral funding falls — US aid through multilateral organisations fell by half — the gap widens: fewer programmes are funded, and the under-provision grows. That is why the article warns of a gap rather than a simple funding shortfall: the market failure is in coordination, and only pooled, multilateral funding can move provision towards Qs.

Marks: 9–10 band — the public-good characteristics are stated, the MSB/MPB gap is explained through the diagram, and under-provision is linked to the article's funding fall. It would fall to the 7–8 band if the diagram were described without explaining why MSB exceeds MPB, or without linking the funding cut to the size of the gap.

Task B model. There is no contradiction, because the two statements describe different things: direction and scale. "Giving more" describes China's direction of travel: its contributions through multilateral channels have risen. "Cannot fill the gap" describes the scale of the hole left by the United States, whose aid through multilateral organisations fell by half, and China's willingness and capacity relative to that hole. Beijing, the article argues, seeks a greater say in the institutions that hand aid out rather than replacing American funding outright. Direction is real; scale is insufficient. Confusing the two is how a true statement, "China gives more", becomes a false conclusion, "China has replaced America".

Marks: 5/5 (Paper 2 short answer) — direction and scale are separated precisely, using the halving of US multilateral aid. It would lose a mark if it confused "giving more" with "replacing America".

Task C model: essay. Multilateral aid pools resources, coordinates donors, and is less tied to any single donor's commercial or political interests, so it can support global public goods such as health and climate programmes. Figure 1 shows why the channel matters: disease control is non-rival and non-excludable, so the marginal social benefit (MSB) lies above the marginal private benefit (MPB). The market provides Qm, where MPB equals marginal cost, but the socially optimal quantity is Qs, where MSB equals marginal cost — the good is under-provided by Qs minus Qm, and only pooled funding moves provision towards Qs. Its weaknesses are speed and accountability: it is slow, bureaucratic, and voting power still reflects donor wealth, so influence follows money even inside a multilateral body. Bilateral aid is faster and donor-controlled, and it can be targeted precisely, but it is often tied to donor exports or contracts, and it fragments recipient planning when many donors pursue separate projects.

Figure 1 — A global public good: disease control. Benefit and cost vertical, quantity (Q) horizontal. MSB lies above MPB, so the market provides Qm but the social optimum is Qs.

The article's evidence sharpens the comparison. The American retreat from multilateral organisations creates a coordination gap that bilateral deals cannot easily replace: fifty bilateral programmes do not add up to one coordinated health system. The WHO case shows it concretely: when the US halved its multilateral aid and withdrew from the WHO while still owing it money, disease-control programmes that depend on pooled surveillance lost funding no bilateral programme replaced — the gap opened even though bilateral giving continued. China's multilateral rise, meanwhile, buys institutional voice, but voice is not the same as development outcomes, and a seat at the table does not guarantee that funds reach the poorest. The evaluation, then, is that effectiveness depends less on the channel than on recipient ownership, transparency, and whether aid builds domestic capacity or creates dependence. The channel matters, but the gap the article describes is a governance gap as much as a funding gap: who decides matters as much as who pays.

Marks: 13–15 band (Paper 1 (b)) — the comparison is structured, Figure 1 is used effectively to show under-provision, article evidence sharpens it (coordination gap, the WHO case, voice versus outcomes), and the conclusion is judged. Closest gap: the bilateral case for speed in emergencies is not worked through a case. Strength: the governance-gap reframing.

## Can Asian governments prevent a food shock? (Sample Volume 01)

# IB EconLens: Single 5 of 5

**Paper 1 (a) · 10 marks** · **Paper 2** · **IA · 14 marks**

# Can Asian governments prevent a food shock?

Asia, 17 October 2026 issue.

IB unit: Microeconomics: 2.2 Supply, 2.3 Competitive market equilibrium, 2.7 Role of government in microeconomics.
Exam link: trains Paper 1 (a) (10 marks) + Paper 2 data response + IA (micro commentary, 14 marks). Paper 3 not covered by this guide.
What it argues. A fierce El Nino is hitting Asian countries already weakened by an energy shock, threatening food supplies; governments must decide whether they can prevent a shock, and how.

Before you read. El Nino is a recurring climate pattern: shifts in Pacific winds bring hotter, drier conditions to much of South and South-East Asia. This episode began in May and is due to peak next month; sea-surface temperature anomalies have already exceeded the peak of every previous event on record. The World Meteorological Organisation expects it to last into February. India's monsoon, which supplies nearly 70% of annual rainfall, ended about 13% below normal, the driest in a decade. Indonesia is enduring its worst fire season for 11 years. Seven provinces in the Philippines are already in drought.

Key vocabulary.
- monsoon: the seasonal wind system that brings most of South Asia's rain.
- drought: a long period with abnormally low rainfall.
- anomaly: a deviation from what is normal or expected.
- havoc: widespread damage or disorder.
- livelihood: the means by which people earn a living.

How to read it.
- The opening lists scattered local events: dead fish in a Cambodian lake, a submerged village exposed in Indonesia, a water warning in Manila. What argument does a list like that build before any data appears?
- Two shocks run through the article: the climate shock and the energy shock. How does the article connect them, and why does that connection matter for policy?
- Reading note. The opening piles up small local events — dead fish in a Cambodian lake, a submerged village exposed in Indonesia, a water warning in Manila — before any data appears. The list shows rather than argues: the shock is already here, in many places. The risk is that anecdote outruns evidence, which is why the article then adds the data, a monsoon 13% below normal and the worst Indonesian fire season in 11 years.

A fierce El Nino is hitting Asian countries already weakened by an energy shock, threatening food supplies.
Tasks.
- A. Paper 1 (a) · 10 marks. Use a supply-and-demand diagram to explain how drought pushes up the price of a staple food.
- B. Paper 2 data response. "El Nino causes food prices to rise" is too short. Write the full chain in your own words (El Nino, drought, harvests, supply, prices), and mark the points where government action could break it.
- C. IA commentary (800 words) — IA · 14 marks. Using this article as your extract, analyse the effect of a supply shock on the market for a staple food, with a supply-and-demand diagram. Evaluate two responses: export bans and subsidies, one against the other.

## Model answers (read after attempting the tasks)

Task A model. Drought reduces harvests, so the supply of a staple food falls. On a supply-and-demand diagram, the supply curve shifts left, from S1 to S2. The equilibrium price rises from P1 to P2 and the equilibrium quantity falls from Q1 to Q2. Because a staple food is a necessity, demand is price-inelastic: the price rises proportionately more than quantity falls, so households spend more for less food. The article's figures show the mechanism: India's monsoon ended about 13% below normal, the driest in a decade, and Indonesia suffered its worst fire season in 11 years. The burden is uneven: low-income households spend a larger share of income on food, so the same price rise hits them hardest. A supply shock, not stronger demand, is what the diagram explains.

Marks: 9–10 band — the shift is correctly linked to drought, the price and quantity effects are stated, inelastic demand is used to explain the size of the price rise, and article data are used. It would fall to the 7–8 band if the elasticity reasoning were missing or the diagram unexplained.

Task B model. El Nino shifts Pacific winds, bringing hotter, drier conditions to South and South-East Asia. The monsoon, which supplies nearly 70% of India's annual rainfall, ends about 13% below normal; drought takes hold in seven Philippine provinces, and Indonesia suffers its worst fire season in 11 years. Harvests fall, so the supply of food shifts left and food prices rise. Because food is a necessity, demand is price-inelastic: the price rise is large, the quantity fall is small, and households spend more for less, with the heaviest burden on low-income families. Governments can break the chain at three points: before the harvest; at the market (targeted cash transfers rather than price ceilings, which discourage supply); and at the border (resisting export bans, which lower domestic prices briefly but cut farmer incentives and export the shock to importers).

Marks: 5/5 (Paper 2 short answer) — the full chain is given with figures, and three points where government can break it are marked. It would lose a mark if the chain stopped at "prices rise" without the intervention points.

Task C model: IA commentary. *Key concept: equity.* Drought shifts the supply of a staple food left, from S1 to S2, on a supply-and-demand diagram (Figure 1). The equilibrium price rises from P1 to P2 and the equilibrium quantity falls from Q1 to Q2. Because a staple is a necessity, demand is price-inelastic: the price rise is proportionately large, the quantity fall is small, and total spending on the staple rises. The diagram shows the size of the shock; equity asks who pays for it. A staple takes a larger share of a low-income household's budget, so the same price rise costs the poorest most, in both money and meals missed. The article's figures show the mechanism: India's monsoon ended about 13% below normal, the driest in a decade, and Indonesia suffered its worst fire season in 11 years.

Figure 1 — The market for a staple food. Price (P) vertical, quantity (Q) horizontal. D1 slopes down, S1 slopes up, meeting at E1 (P1, Q1). Drought shifts supply left to S2; new equilibrium E2.

Two responses can be evaluated, and equity is the test that separates them. Export bans help domestic consumers briefly by keeping food at home, but they reduce farmer incomes and incentives, which lowers future supply, and they push prices up for import-dependent neighbours. That is a beggar-thy-neighbour policy: it exports the shock, invites retaliation, and can spiral into a wider crisis — it buys equity at home by imposing inequity abroad. Subsidies and transfers, by contrast, protect consumers without destroying the price signal: targeted cash transfers to low-income households are more efficient than universal subsidies, because they reach those who need help without subsidising those who do not. Their limit is fiscal: they strain government budgets already weakened by the energy shock. The shock itself cannot be prevented by policy, but its human cost can be limited. The best response protects the vulnerable without breaking the market signals farmers need to plant again next season — it shares the burden rather than shifting it.

Marks: 14/14 — A 3/3 (Figure 1 drawn, fully labelled, explained in the text), B 2/2, C 3/3, D 3/3 (equity named and carried through — who pays, export bans, targeting), E 3/3 (export bans and transfers genuinely weighed, fiscal limit noted). Strength: the beggar-thy-neighbour evaluation. Watch-point: the fiscal limit is noted, not quantified.

---

## China's exports of clean tech to South-East Asia are soaring (Volume 02 (free guide))

# IB EconLens: Single 1 of 5

**Paper 1 (a) · 10 marks** · **Paper 2** · **IA · 14 marks**

## How to use this single

Read the original first, then work through the guide. Attempt the tasks before reading the model answers.

# China's exports of clean tech to South-East Asia are soaring

China, 14 November 2026 issue.

IB unit: The global economy: 4.1 Benefits of international trade, 4.2 Types of trade protection.
Best IB use: IA commentary (global).
Exam link: trains Paper 1 (a) (10 marks) + Paper 2 data response + IA (global commentary, 14 marks). Paper 3 not covered by this guide.

What it argues. Chinese clean-technology exports are shifting rapidly from Europe to South-East Asia, where governments welcome rather than resist them. Europe is curbing the inflow while South-East Asian demand surges, sharpened by the war over the Strait of Hormuz.

Before you read. Chinese producers once looked mainly to Europe, but European governments have begun restricting the inflow. Meanwhile, exports to South-East Asia have risen fast: in the first nine months of 2026, China's exports of solar technology to the region rose by almost 60%, while exports to Europe fell by 11%. Indonesia's president has promised to raise solar capacity from about 1.5 GW to 100 GW by 2029.

Key vocabulary.
- clean technology (clean tech): equipment that produces energy with low or no carbon emissions.
- tariff: a tax on imported goods, raising their price.
- quota: a limit on the quantity that may be imported.

How to read it.
- Reading note. The author opens with Europe — the market readers expect, where the story is about resistance — before turning to South-East Asia, where the same exports meet a welcome. The contrast is the argument: the flow is driven by the policy and industrial context in each destination, not by the product alone. The Philippines, with little domestic industry that feels threatened, shows the point: its priority is building renewable capacity as fast as possible.

Chinese clean-technology exports are shifting rapidly from Europe to South-East Asia, where governments welcome rather than resist them.
Tasks.
- A. Paper 1 (a) · 10 marks. Using a supply-and-demand diagram, explain how the war over the Strait of Hormuz affected the market for solar panels in South-East Asia.
- B. Logic (Paper 2 data response). The article gives two different explanations for rising South-East Asian demand: the war shock and the region's own energy goals. What does that distinction do to a simple "the war caused it" reading? Name the two causes, and explain why each matters for how long the boom will last.
- C. IA commentary (800 words) — IA · 14 marks. Using this article as your extract, analyse the effects of European trade protection on the market for Chinese clean technology in Europe, with a supply-and-demand diagram. Evaluate whether South-East Asia gains or loses from the resulting redirection of Chinese exports.

## Model answers (read after attempting the tasks)

Task A model. Solar panels are a substitute for oil- and gas-fired electricity. When fighting over the Strait of Hormuz choked supplies from the Gulf, electricity prices in South-East Asia rose, so households and firms looked for cheaper power, and demand for solar panels rose. On a supply-and-demand diagram for solar panels, the demand curve shifts right, from D1 to D2. The equilibrium price rises from P1 to P2 and the equilibrium quantity rises from Q1 to Q2. The article's numbers fit this: exports of solar technology to the region rose by almost 60% in nine months, and the Philippines became the world's second-largest buyer of Chinese panels. This is a change in demand, not a movement along the curve — and if the war shock fades, demand would shift back, which is why the region's own energy targets matter more.

Marks: 9–10 band — the substitute mechanism is fully explained, the demand shift is distinguished from a movement along the curve, the diagram is described with labelled shifts (D1 to D2, P1 to P2, Q1 to Q2), and the article's evidence (the 60% rise) is tied to the shift. The diagram is described here and must be drawn and labelled; without it, the 7–8 band.

Task B model. Two causes must be kept separate. First, the war shock: fighting over the Strait of Hormuz has choked Gulf oil and gas supplies, pushing up electricity prices. Second, the region's own energy goals: governments want energy security and more renewable capacity. The distinction matters because the two imply different durations: a war shock may reverse, so war-driven demand could fall back, while policy-driven demand is more durable.

Marks: 4/5 (Paper 2 short answer) — both causes are named and the duration argument follows from each. The lost mark: it does not say which cause drives the 60% rise, treating the two as equal.

Task C model: IA commentary. The key concept is *interdependence*: Europe, China and South-East Asia are linked through one market, so a policy decision in one place moves prices and quantities in the others, and no government controls the outcome alone. That link runs through the whole analysis below.

European protection restricts supply: a quota limits the quantity that can enter, and a tariff raises its price. On a supply-and-demand diagram for Chinese clean technology in Europe, the supply curve shifts left, from S1 to S2. The equilibrium price rises from P1 to P2 and the equilibrium quantity falls from Q1 to Q2 — the 11% fall in exports to Europe in the first nine months of 2026.

Diagram — market for Chinese clean technology in Europe (draw this).
- Axes: price (P) vertical; quantity (Q) horizontal.
- Curves: demand D downward; supply S1 upward, shifting left to S2.
- Equilibria: E1 (P1, Q1) where D meets S1; E2 (P2, Q2) where D meets S2.
- Result: P2 above P1; Q2 below Q1. Welfare: consumer-surplus loss exceeds producer gain plus tariff revenue; the gap is deadweight loss.

In Europe: domestic producers gain from less competition and higher prices, while consumers lose — they pay more, and some are priced out altogether. The consumer loss exceeds the producer gain plus any government revenue, leaving a deadweight loss.

Interdependence then shows up on the other side of the world. Supply that cannot enter Europe is redirected: in South-East Asia the supply of Chinese panels and batteries rises, so prices there fall and quantities rise — solar exports to the region rose by almost 60% in nine months, and the Philippines became the world's second-largest buyer of Chinese panels. South-East Asia gains cheaper electricity and faster renewable growth, and Indonesia's plan to raise solar capacity from about 1.5 GW to 100 GW by 2029 becomes cheaper to deliver. But the gain is borrowed from Europe's policy. Some of the flow is repackaged and sold on to Western markets, helping China avoid tariffs and exposing the region to retaliation. And if the war over the Strait of Hormuz ends and Gulf energy becomes cheap again, the demand that pulled the panels in could fade as fast as it arrived.

The evaluation is mixed but leans positive in the short run: South-East Asia gains cheaper energy and faster renewable growth, but the gain rests on fragile foundations — a war-driven price shock and a tariff-evasion route — neither of which the region controls.

Marks: 13/14 — A 3/3 (diagram block: axes, D, S1 to S2, E1/E2, P1–P2, Q1–Q2, deadweight loss, all explained in the text); B 2/2; C 3/3 (Europe and South-East Asia traced through supply shifts; 60% and 11% figures); D 3/3 (interdependence linked through redirection and evaluation); E 2/3 (clear short-run judgement, but no firm long-run verdict).

## Europe living beyond its means (Volume 03 (free guide))

# IB EconLens: Single 1 of 5

**Paper 1 (a) · 10 marks** · **Paper 2** · **IA · 14 marks**

## How to use this single

Read the original first, then work through the guide. Ask three questions: (1) What is the author's argument? (2) How is it built? (3) Where is it weakest? Attempt the tasks before reading the model answers.

# Europe living beyond its means

Europe, 14 November 2026 issue.

IB unit: 3.6 Fiscal policy: government spending, taxation, budget deficits and government debt. *Also useful:* 3.5 Monetary policy — higher interest rates raise the cost of servicing government debt.
Best IB use: IA commentary (macro) or Paper 1 essay evidence.

Exam link: trains Paper 1 (a) (10 marks) + Paper 2 data response + IA (macro commentary, 14 marks). Paper 3 not covered by this guide.

What it argues. Europe spends far more on pensions and welfare than it can afford, and the gap is now catching up with it. Five countries carry public debt at or above 100% of GDP, and ten are under the EU's excessive-deficit procedure. Yet fragmented parliaments and populist politics make the needed cuts almost impossible to agree.

Before you read. EU countries devote nearly 30% of GDP to public social spending, against less than 20% in America, and 10% of GDP to public pensions, nearly twice the American share. In France, the government plans to cut the deficit from 5.4% of GDP in 2026 to 5% in 2027, including a freeze in nominal terms on most pensions and civil-service pay — while 85% of French voters say curbing debt is urgent, 56% also say the pension age should be lower.

Key vocabulary.
- budget deficit: the amount by which government spending exceeds tax revenue in a given year.
- government (public) debt: the total amount a government owes, built up from past budget deficits.
- debt-to-GDP ratio: government debt expressed as a percentage of GDP; used to judge whether debt is sustainable.
- excessive-deficit procedure: the EU process for countries breaking the debt and deficit rules.

How to read it.
- The article tours countries from the most strained to the most worrying. For each, ask two questions: how big is the fiscal gap, and what stops the government closing it?

Reading note: The author builds the argument by touring countries — Belgium, where a government collapses over a budget; Germany, where even a debt-brake country faces a crunch; France, the climax, with three hostile blocs, a pension freeze and populists promising the opposite. Each case adds a different political form of the same fiscal problem, so read each country for the size of the fiscal gap and what stops the government closing it.
Europe wants a level of public spending it can no longer afford, and its fractured politics cannot agree the cuts — so the bond markets may end up imposing them.
Tasks.
- A. Paper 1 (a) · 10 marks. Use an AD/AS diagram to explain how the French government's planned fiscal consolidation — spending cuts including a freeze on pensions and civil-service pay — affects real GDP and the price level in France in the short run.
- B. Paper 2 data response (short answer). The article says most French voters think curbing debt is urgent, yet most also want a lower pension age, and populist leaders promise to protect pensions and cut the retirement age. What does this contradiction do to the claim that the problem is simply that governments lack the will to act? Explain whose incentives are in conflict.
- C. IA commentary (800 words) — IA · 14 marks. Using this article as your extract, analyse the effects of the French government's planned fiscal consolidation — spending cuts including a freeze on pensions and civil-service pay — on the French economy, with an AD/AS diagram. Evaluate whether cutting spending is the best way to reduce the budget deficit.

## Model answers (read after attempting the tasks)

Task A model. Fiscal consolidation through spending cuts is a contractionary fiscal policy: lower government spending (G) is a component of aggregate demand, so AD shifts left. On an AD/AS diagram (real GDP on the horizontal axis, price level on the vertical axis), AD shifts from AD1 to AD2 along an upward-sloping SRAS, moving the equilibrium from E1 to E2. Real GDP falls from Y1 to Y2 and the price level falls from PL1 to PL2, so the policy is contractionary and deflationary in the short run. The fall in GDP is likely to be large because pensioners and public-sector workers have a high marginal propensity to consume, so freezing their incomes cuts consumption sharply and the multiplier magnifies the initial fall in G. This is the short run only: SRAS does not shift.

Marks: 9–10 band — theory fully explained, diagram complete (axes, AD1 to AD2, E1 to E2, Y1 to Y2, PL1 to PL2), terminology accurate; draw and label the diagram in the exam — an undrawn diagram falls to 7–8.

Task B model. The contradiction shifts the blame from governments to voters, and that changes the logic. If the problem were only weak leadership, a braver government could fix it; but the poll evidence shows voters themselves demand both lower debt and more generous pensions. That is why the warning lands on the bond markets: when democratic politics cannot resolve the contradiction, rising borrowing costs eventually will.

Marks: 4/5 (Paper 2 short answer). Strength: the voter contradiction is tied to conflicting incentives. Loses 1 mark: the poll evidence is stated generally, without the article's figures.

Task C model: IA commentary. The key concept is equity: who bears the cost of fixing the public finances, and who gains. France's plan — cutting the deficit from 5.4% of GDP in 2026 to 5% in 2027, including a freeze in nominal terms on most pensions and civil-service pay — puts the adjustment on today's pensioners and public-sector workers, while the benefit, lower debt, accrues mainly to future taxpayers.

Diagram — AD/AS, France. Draw this:
Axes: real GDP (horizontal), price level (vertical). Curves: downward-sloping AD, upward-sloping SRAS. Shift: AD1 to AD2 (left). Equilibria: E1 to E2. Real GDP falls Y1 to Y2; price level falls PL1 to PL2. Label every axis, curve and point.

On the diagram, lower government spending (G) cuts aggregate demand, so AD shifts left along SRAS to lower output and a lower price level: contractionary and deflationary in the short run. The fall in GDP is likely to be large, because pensioners and public-sector workers have a high marginal propensity to consume, so freezing their incomes cuts consumption sharply and the multiplier magnifies the initial fall in G. Households lose real income; the government gains fiscal space and pays less interest — 91 billion euros in 2027, up from 79 billion in 2026 — but only if the cuts stick.

Equity is where the plan is hardest to defend. A pension freeze falls on people with fixed incomes who cannot easily work longer, while raising taxes instead would spread the cost more widely, and raising the pension age would put it on future retirees. Yet doing nothing is not equitable either: debt at 112% of GDP means future taxpayers inherit the bill, and impatient bond markets would impose the adjustment as higher interest rates. The voters are asking for both sides of the bargain at once: 85% call curbing debt urgent, while 56% want a lower pension age.

The cuts are therefore necessary but inequitable in how they fall, and politically fragile — France has had four prime ministers in three years. The freeze is defensible as a first step, since pensions are the largest budget item, but without reforms voters accept, the deficit will return. Cutting spending is the least bad option, not a solution: it buys time at today's pensioners' cost, and time only helps if used for reforms that share the burden more fairly.

Marks: 13/14 — A 3/3 (diagram complete, labelled, explained), B 2/2, C 3/3 (multiplier chain traced to article data), D 3/3 (equity carried through who pays, who gains, the alternatives), E 2/3 (judgement clear, but the long-run growth channel is stated, not weighed).
